England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group.
But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina .
First of all the context of the two games was entirely different.
England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players.
Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on.
But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White.
Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano.
Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford.
"Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners."
60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages
Making defensive subs is fine when it works - but when it does not, boy will a manager hear about it.
In the World Cup last 16, England had been 2-1 up against Mexico in the Azteca when Jarell Quansah was sent off.
Tuchel brought on three defenders for a defender, a midfielder and a forward.
But England won 3-2 and Dan Burn's cameo was the stuff of legend.
However, nine days later with England 1-0 up against Argentina, Tuchel did the same again - three defenders on for a defender, midfielder and forward.
The first of those subs, with Konsa replacing Anthony Gordon, was in the 72nd minute.
And England just sat back until Argentina broke their resistance.
However, against Spain this time, despite England being down to 10 men and facing incessant pressure, Tuchel was not so quick with defensive subs.
Myles Lewis-Skelly, replacing Harry Kane, was the first on after 78 minutes - 15 minutes after Anderson's sending off. And then five minutes later he brought on two more players - but one of them was a striker in Dominic Calvert-Lewin.
"Harry played 78 minutes, Jude [Bellingham] 83 minutes and then just defending and defending, it's tiring," explained Tuchel.
"So we needed fresh energy. I was asked yesterday what happens if there needs to be a critical or crucial substitution. And I said, I feel free enough to take any substitution if I think it is necessary to help the team and to influence the game.
"I feel free enough to do that and I think there was a lot of defending needed. So we just went for some fresh legs."
Dan Burn usually comes on when England are trying to hang on - but he was only introduced for the last few minutes
England actually faced more of a siege this time than against the Argentines, the stats confirm.
In the final 30 minutes they faced 19 shots from Spain, with seven on target and an expected goals (xG) total of 2.53.
Argentina, in that time, had 10 shots, with four on target and an xG of 1.41.
In terms of passes from England the numbers were similar with 65 against Argentina and 61 against Spain - both times with an accuracy rate of about 64%.
In Thursday's 2-1 win against Croatia , as a comparison, they tried 557 passes with accuracy of 89%.
"For half an hour it was Mexico reloaded and it felt like we were back in the Azteca. We had to overcome 30 minutes which, against Spain, felt like three hours," Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"The difficult thing is it's not only a red card, it's a red card, and a goal so that makes a completely new game. Thirty minutes against the world champion feels like three hours. I said it before in the stadium and wave after wave after wave."
England were criticised for blowing a 2-1 half-time lead at Wembley in their first Nations League game with Spain .
But on that day their final 30-minute figurers were much better - with only five shots faced and 176 attempted passes with a 90% accuracy.
So what was different this time? Perhaps the team showed more resilience and unity?
After Spain had pulled one back England's players had a huddle.
"I love the fact the team went into a huddle and if anything the manager's stepped back because he wants to see the player reaction," said ex-England defender Matt Upson on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"I almost think that the trauma from that sending off of Elliot Anderson has almost been a positive thing for England because it's given the team a chance to get together and cope in what is an incredibly difficult situation and come through the other side.
"There was so much going on in this game. England had to suffer and came through the other side."
Defender and goalscorer White was asked about the huddle after the game.
"Just stay calm, when you're one down it becomes more difficult and things change so it was all about managing that," he said.
Another factor was the performance of England keeper James Trafford, who made six saves - with four of them coming in the final 12 minutes of the game with the score at 3-2.
He made an incredible double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in injury time.
Upson said: "I think that double save was the moment for Spain and Trafford had the answers."

Arsenal Women vs London City Lionesses. Barclays Women's Super League.
Report and free match highlights as Arsenal's wait for a home WSL win goes on after a 1-1 draw against London City Lionesses; the Gunners have now drawn all five games at the Emirates this season; Frida Maanum's early strike was immediately cancelled out by Izzy Goodwin
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Arsenal's wait for a home WSL win continues as they drew 1-1 against London City Lionesses on Sunday - their fifth draw in a row at the Emirates this season - with an inspired Mary Earps denying the Gunners victory.
While the result extends Arsenal's unbeaten home run to 24 league matches, it is becoming an increasing concern and a spectre on the shoulder that the Gunners have been unable to secure three points at the Emirates this year.
Giving her view to Sky Sports after the game, Renee Slegers - managing her 50th Arsenal game - said: "We spent more time than we normally do without the ball; partly the game plan and partly them asking questions of us on the pitch.
"We create big chances, could have done more with those. That's the frustrating part. This is the fifth [home game] and we couldn't give the fans the win. Unfortunately we couldn't do it for them."
It was two early goals that decided the fixture too. Frida Maanum scored for a second game in a row - having netted against Barcelona in the Champions League in midweek - slotting home from an Alessia Russo cross to put Arsenal ahead.
But a minute later, London City were level. Leah Williamson lost the run of the lively Izzy Goodwin, and the striker lashed into the roof of the net.
From then on, it was a goalkeeping masterclass from former England No 1 Earps especially that kept Arsenal from scoring another with her counterpart Misa Rodriguez also making her fair share of saves, albeit not as frequently.
The Gunners simply could not find a way past the inspired London City stopper as Lionesses boss Sarina Wiegman watched on from the stands.
The pick of her string of world-class saves came when she tipped a Maanum shot onto the crossbar. It came shortly after substitute Delphine Cascarino had also rattled the woodwork at the other end.
The result does little to improve either side's WSL standings, and Arsenal's hopes of finishing in the Champions League places takes another hit. They are sixth on 14 points - already six behind London City in third.
"We were happy with the one point, we wanted and needed three today," Slegers added. "Every game is three points for Arsenal when we play for this club.
"At the moment, with our position in the table and how we need to stay connected and compete for the top three positions for the Champions League, this one was very important for us.
"With that being said, the season isn't over. It's still November and we have to look at what it looks like in May."
10: GOAL! A sweeping move is finished by Maanum after Russo's cutback to give Arsenal the lead.
11: GOAL! London City immediately equalise as Goodwin fires into the roof of the net.
22: SAVE! Earps makes a good stop to deny Lisa Baum, who cuts in from the right-hand side.
27: SAVE! Misa Rodriguez on hand this time to deny Alexia Putellas.
29: SAVE! Again from Earps! This time it's a flying effort to keep out another Baum shot.
68: CROSSBAR! Cascarino pings an effort off the top of the woodwork.
77: DOUBLE SAVE! Earps pulls off another brilliant double save, first to deny Smith then Maanum.
85: CROSSBAR! Earps fingertips a Maanum shot onto the crossbar.
Before Sunday's game, S ky Sports asked whether Arsenal have lost their fear factor at the Emirates this season.
The answer surely has to be yes - although after the game, Slegers was adamant that the fear factor has not gone, despite being without a win.
Teams have come to the Emirates and sat in a low block that the Gunners have been unable to break down more than once.
London City were never going to do that. It's not in their DNA. They closer resemble the Barcelona team Arsenal faced on Thursday where, funnily enough, they drew 1-1.
But what they might not have been banking on was an ingenious performance from Earps. While Arsenal did not have to worry about defenders sitting back, they did face a goalkeeper putting in one of the performances of the season. How's your luck?
She made eight saves as Arsenal continued to pepper her goal - her most in the WSL since 2017 - and the second-most in the WSL this season after the goalkeeper that replaces her at Man Utd, Phallon Tullis-Joyce.
When asked how she found the game, Earps told Sky Sports: "Tiring. It's a big point away from home.
"Either team could have won it in terms of chances. Happy with the point - would have liked three. All the girls put their bodies on the line. I love defending. It was tough today and I thought we did a good job."
It was perhaps made all the sweeter for her that her former England boss Sarina Wiegman was watching on. It is well-documented how she departed the national team, but it certainly showed the Lionesses head coach what she was missing.
Earps has had to bide her time at London City, with Elene Lete continuing to be the No 1 until recently. The former England No 1 has now started in three games, and while she is yet to keep a clean sheet, she will have staked a huge claim to the permeant spot with her performance on Sunday.
"Mary is amazing," her boss Eder Maestre said after the game. "It's not just because of the talent she has, she delivers the commitment and the togetherness that she can bring to the team because of her experience. Watching her in that performance was a pleasure."
" Two good teams going against each other. I think we started the game well, score a very good goal, but we let them come back into the game too easily.
"I must say the players left everything on the pitch. They were absolutely dedicated, playing with hunger and focus. There are things in our game we must do better. We want to be dominating the ball. Being more ruthless. It's very basic but that's what it's about."
On Maanum: "She was very big for us against Barcelona and good for us tonight again. You can always count on her with runs into the box. The finish was very good."
On 50th Arsenal game: "I'm proud to represent Arsenal. I want to do everything I can for Arsenal."
"We are happy because this kind of environment is always difficult to cope with, but at the same time, we want to win every game so we cannot be [too happy] just because it's the first time we've drawn against Arsenal.
"Our targets are even bigger. We have the hop to have the performance. We improve quite well in the second half. We had the chances, and they did as well.
"They're one of the best teams in the world and playing knowing that they need the points to push for the Champions League positions. We already knew how close it was going to be."

Arsenal’s fifth draw from five home games in the Women’s Super League left them frustrated once again but this was a wholly different story to the previous four, as they played out an entertaining 1-1 draw with a London City Lionesses side inspired by their goalkeeper Mary Earps.
Aston Villa, Birmingham, Manchester United and Crystal Palace all came to this stadium for a point, defending resolutely and exposing Arsenal’s inability to break down low blocks, whereas London City came to play and were rewarded with a draw that maintains their six‑point advantage over Arsenal in the race for a European place, and moving within six points of the leaders Chelsea.
Earps, producing her best performance to date for the team she joined in the summer, repeatedly denied Frida Maanum and Lisa Baum and was named player of the match in a contest where both goals were scored inside the space of 99 seconds. The impressive Maanum finished off a superb team move for Arsenal to open the scoring in the 10th minute but her goal was cancelled out by a terrific finish from Isobel Goodwin whose head coach, Eder Maestre, said: “We came here to take risks. We really wanted to win.
“Our identity is playing with bravery – we were brave today. We weren’t scared about the context, the opponent, the stadium, nothing. We tried to play as we play at home.”
Arsenal had secured an impressive result in Barcelona on Thursday, drawing with the European champions , but this game against the WSL’s third-placed side felt as though it was of even greater importance, particularly if Arsenal wish to continue visiting venues such as the Camp Nou next season, and they were unable to find a way past Earps to win and close the gap in the table.
Just like they had done away at Anfield last Sunday , Renée Slegers’s team made a bright start with energy, pace and the threat of Alessia Russo. Emily Fox’s shot was deflected wide, after a good move that included some excellent Maanum buildup play, before Ona Batlle’s long-range effort bounced wide. It was not long before Maanum tucked in the opening goal after an intelligent cutback from Russo.
The visitors struck back almost immediately, though, as Goodwin did superbly to turn inside Leah Williamson and then demonstrated strength and composure to hold off Baum and fire a lethal finish past Misa Rodríguez with power and precision. It was a timely moment of class from the English striker in front of the England head coach, Sarina Wiegman, who was in the stands before naming her next England squad on Tuesday morning.
Earps then twice saved from Baum from range. After the break, Earps did well again to dive low to her left to divert a Caitlin Foord strike wide, and what followed was a sustained spell of London City possession, territory and chances. Maestre’s team spent a good part of 20 minutes firmly camped in Arsenal’s half and they carved open a good chance for Kadidiatou Diani but her relatively tame, low, near-post effort was saved by Rodríguez.
Diani’s 62nd-minute replacement from the substitutes’ bench, Delphine Cascarino, drew gasps from the crowd as she unleashed a dipping strike that bounced off the top of the crossbar. It was a lucky escape for Arsenal, who had won all seven of their previous meetings with London City across all competitions but were denied by two more fine Earps stops, firstly from a Maanum close-range effort and then from Maanum’s curler, which looked destined for the top corner before Earps touched it on to the bar.
Viviane Asseyi scored twice as West Ham secured back-to-back WSL home wins after beating rock-bottom Charlton 2-0.
Asseyi’s curled finish put the Irons in front just ahead of the break and she then scored a 25-yard free-kick early in the second half. The defeat saw Charlton, who remain without a point, become the first WSL team to lose all 10 of their opening matches of the season.
Mathilde Harviken’s late goal gave Aston Villa a 1-0 win over derby rivals Birmingham , which gives Brian Sørensen his third win since stepping in as interim manager and leaves his side seventh. Press Association
Slegers’s 50th WSL match in charge of the north London side almost ended in defeat late on but Alexia Putellas’s rising, stoppage-time strike flew narrowly over the bar. Regarding lying sixth in the table after 10 games, Slegers said “the season isn’t over, it’s still November”, before praising her team’s resurgence in their past three matches.
“The team is in a very good place,” she said. “The preparation, the dedication, the hunger for details, doing everything they possibly can – that’s the standard. Things are clicking well. But also the [opponents], they’re teams that spend time on the ball and that are brave and want to dominate games, so the types of games have been different.”
It certainly was different but the end result was the same for an Arsenal team still unable to find that elusive home win.

Ronaldinho played 45 minutes on his return to professional football in Italy. The 46-year-old Brazil great announced in June that he had signed for the Serie C side Ravenna, 11 years after he appeared to have brought his illustrious career to a close with Fluminense.
Five months later, he was in the starting lineup as Ravenna faced their local rivals Forlì. Ronaldinho, wearing the No 10 shirt, entered the stadium to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Stadio Bruno Benelli adding a temporary 1,800-capacity stand – dubbed “R10” – for the occasion. Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli’s Con Te Partiro blasted out of the stadium’s speakers.
Ronaldinho failed to add to his goal tally upon his return, showing some nice touches and playing a role in helping Giulio Donati score Ravenna’s opening goal, but unable to create a sight of goal for himself.
The 2005 Ballon d’Or winner acknowledged the Ravenna fans at the end of the first half and was replaced by Matteo Maggio when the teams returned after the break.
Ronaldinho, who has also become a shareholder in the club, hinted there could be more appearances to come, telling Sky Italia: “It went by too fast, that has always been football for me. Is this my last one? I don’t know. If the president keeps calling me, I will come back. It is always a pleasure. I told the president, if he needs me, then I will be here.
“It was lovely to be here, playing, having the buildup in the dressing room. Football has always been the most wonderful thing in my life.”
Ravenna, who have not played in Serie B since 2008, are second in their regional group in Serie C and came into the weekend’s fixtures six points behind the leaders, Spezia.
It is Ronaldinho’s second spell in Italy, albeit at a much lower level, after three seasons with Milan from 2008 to 2011, where he won one Serie A title. He also played for Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona in a trophy-laden career that included claiming the World Cup with Brazil in 2002. He scored 94 goals in 207 matches for Barcelona and 33 times in 97 games for Brazil. He has also played for Brazilian sides Grêmio, Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, and for Querétaro in Mexico.

Ronaldinho played the first 45 minutes for Ravenna against Forli
Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their 2-0 win over Forli in an Italian third-tier derby.
The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.
He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.
The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.
He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.
At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.
Ronaldinho was substituted at the break with the score at 1-0.
A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.
The game was streamed in several countries around the world.
Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.
A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.
In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.
He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.
He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.
Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.
"It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia.
And asked if he might play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group, he said: "If the president calls me, I'll be back."
All of Ravenna's players - and not just the starting XI - posed with Ronaldinho in the team photo before kick-off

Match report as England secure a stunning 3-2 win over Spain to end the world champions' 43-game unbeaten run and finish top of Nations League Group A3; Three Lions raced into a three-goal lead then clung on after Elliot Anderson's red card
England withstood a Spain fightback after Elliot Anderson's red card to secure a famous 3-2 victory and finish above the world champions at the top of their Nations League group.
Thomas Tuchel's side were sensational for an hour in Madrid, taking the lead when Harry Kane scored a penalty at the end of the first half and then adding quickfire goals from Ezri Konsa and Ben White.
But a one-sided game was turned on its head when Elliot Anderson was sent off for a last-man foul on Lamine Yamal following Jarell Quansah's error, allowing Mikel Oyarzabal to score from the spot.
Spain reduced the deficit to one goal when substitute Nico Williams converted Lamine Yamal's cross after Anthony Gordon had been dispossessed, but England clung on thanks to James Trafford.
The goalkeeper, selected ahead of Jordan Pickford, made a string of saves as Spain peppered the England goal, including a stunning double stop when he denied Fermin Lopez then somehow pushed Oyarzabal's follow-up around the post at full stretch.
His heroics, in addition to a vital last-man challenge by White on Williams, allowed the Three Lions to end Spain's 43-game unbeaten run with a historic victory which ensures they will be seeded in the Nations League quarter-final draw.
It appeared certain to be a more emphatic victory when White drilled the third goal through the legs of Unai Simon after Konsa had headed in Declan Rice's corner for the second. Spain had not even registered a shot on target at that point.
But Anderson's red card, after Quansah was caught on the ball by Lamine Yamal, reinvigorated Spain and meant England had to show the qualities demonstrated in their World Cup last-16 win over Mexico at the Azteca Stadium in July.
Their steel, and the contribution of their goalkeeper, got them over the line - and showed evidence of progress from their World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina, when they lost their lead late on.
"We are fully aware of the performance we put out there for 60-65 minutes. To be 3-0 up and deservedly 3-0 up.
"Of course the red card and penalty changed the momentum and the characteristic of the game. Thirty minutes against Spain, in Spain, feels like three hours.
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
"That is the statement and significance of this victory: that it was deserved and the result followed the performance.
"It was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit and togetherness. It was on highest level football wise on all aspects of the game.
"That was an excellent performance. A wonderful feeling in the dressing room. Everyone was very tired. We overcame some difficult moments.
"We're aware what steps we took now after the World Cup. It's the best feeling."
"We knew we could beat them. We knew we were going to beat them today.
"The message from the manager after the Croatia game was so positive. The message from the boys, everyone pushing together, knowing that we're going to come here and not sit back and hit them on the counter.
"We knew from the first minute - our first 10 minutes was probably the best we've played in a 10-minute spell. Pressure, pressure, pressure, we could have had two or three.
"The red card changes the course of the game as it could have been a couple more goals if I'm being honest."
England's football DNA has been in focus this autumn. In Madrid, we saw the English style at its best. From the first whistle, England were boldly on the front foot, overwhelming Spain with pace, power and directness.
They snapped into tackles and gave short shrift to their opponents when they called for fouls. It was physical, it was aggressive. It was certainly not England trying to replicate the Spanish style.
The set-piece routine for the second goal was a reflection of how they have risen in importance in the Premier League and fittingly saw two Arsenal players combine to score it. Then, when down to 10 men, there was fight, heart and commitment.
Roy Keane called England's performance "perfect" at half-time. The errors from Quansah, Anderson and Gordon meant it certainly couldn't be called that in the end. But England's attitude and approach outweighed their mistakes.
England find out who they will face in the Nations League quarter-finals when the draw takes place on Friday November 20 at 11am.
The two-legged ties are scheduled for the March international break, with the first legs to be played between March 25 and 27 and the second legs between March 28 and 30.

Scotland delivered a first home win under Sebastien Pocognoli on Friday but a stodgy 2-1 against North Macedonia did little to lift the frustrated mood of fans.
Now the Nations League campaign concludes with a visit to runaway group winners Switzerland.
Scotland must win in St Gallen to have any chance of leapfrogging Slovenia into second place and the promotion play-offs.
It will also determine their seeding for the impending Euro 2028 draw. Falling into pot three less than a year after topping a World Cup qualifying group would be a huge backward step.
So is it time to let the shackles off and go for broke or would it be more prudent to adopt a defensive strategy and hope to sucker the Swiss on the break or from a set-piece?
Put yourself in Pocognoli's shoes and pick an XI with our team selector below, while we have picked out some of the key selection dilemmas.
Pocognoli has settled on a 3-4-2-1 formation but the approach is far from convincing, with a lack of threat from the flanks among the issues facing the Belgian.
On the left, there are question marks about the quality of Andy Robertson's deliveries in recent times. On the right, natural winger Ben Gannon-Doak has looked entirely uncomfortable.
Would it be more effective to use them in their regular club positions? Pocognoli has intimated that he is not married to the system, telling BBC Scotland he will try "to find the best shape to make the players shine on the pitch.
"I always try to adapt to my team. I think the shape that we play is the best shape to fit the best quality of the team."
If he is going to stick with three at the back, does Kieran Tierney perhaps have a better delivery than Robertson? Is a three at the back system the only way to accommodate both?
Either way, Robertson is going to start and he's going to become the nation's most capped player.
Full-backs Aaron Hickey and Nathan Patterson are certainly more used to defending than Gannon-Doak, but can they be relied upon to provide a cutting edge in the final third?
On a largely-exasperating evening, Gannon-Doak did earn the penalty that brought victory on Friday. If the boss sticks to his guns, could his speed and direct running be utilised behind a striker instead of out wide?
Tough watch as Scotland again battle against their own limitations
Che Adams was reinstated straight into the starting line-up by Pocognoli after missing the new head coach's first international window through injury.
While he didn't get on the scoresheet, his subtle bump on a North Macedonian defender led to John McGinn's first goal and his combination play with Scott McTominay was noticeable.
Hull City striker Oli McBurnie started the first four games of the Pocognoli era after ending his long exile from the squad and earned praise for his industry, but he remains without an international goal.
However, it was McBurnie who was chosen to replace Adams after 66 minutes with Kieron Bowie left on the bench and Robbie Ure omitted from the matchday squad.
Could his slightly more robust approach be a better foil for the likes of Scott McTominay and John McGinn?
Or will Pocognoli stick with Torino striker Adams, who has four goals in nine Serie A games this season?
Speaking of Serie A Scots, Bologna midfielder Lewis Ferguson has played every single minute under Pocognoli - the only outfield player to achieve that feat.
Billy Gilmour has started next to Ferguson in midfield in all of five of those games, with the head coach keen for the Napoli man to play a little higher up the pitch instead of in the deep-lying role he played under Steve Clarke.
Again, there have been questions about the effectiveness of the pair. Ferguson was arguably Scotland's best player in a poor World Cup display and his ball-winning prowess might suit the Switzerland game.
But no player in the English Premier League has won the ball back more in the opposition half than Ryan Christie.
The former Inverness, Aberdeen and Celtic midfielder was more known for his attacking intent but over the last 18 months, he has been moved to a deeper, more central role in a flying Bournemouth team.
He recently captained the Cherries to a 3-0 win over AC Milan, has started of three of the last four in Bournemouth's unbeaten league run, and began in the 3-0 win over McGinn's Aston Villa in the League Cup.
He reached his 75th cap coming off the bench against North Macedonia but has started just once under Pocognoli, in the 2-1 loss against Slovenia.
Is there a place for him in this team? Who would drop out if that were the case? Or is there a way for Pocognoli to name all five big midfielder - including McGinn and McTominay - at once?

James Trafford made a string of impressive saves to help England claim a 3-2 win over Spain in the Nations League; Leeds goalkeeper was picked ahead of Jordan Pickford at the Metropolitano Stadium, so is he Thomas Tuchel's man now?
Do England have a new No 1? Thomas Tuchel insists not. "There's no No 1," he said. But Jordan Pickford might have his work cut out to wrestle the shirt back from James Trafford on the evidence of his performance in England's 3-2 win over Spain.
It felt significant that he started in the first place. Pickford has been England's undisputed first choice for a decade; an outstanding servant to the national team whose total of 94 caps puts him behind only Peter Shilton among the most-capped goalkeepers.
But this was undoubtedly England's biggest test of their Nations League campaign and Tuchel opted for Trafford, encouraged by his displays at home to Spain and away to Czech Republic in September. "He had a brilliant match," he added afterwards.
If it is a changing of the guard, then it is being handled carefully. "I think it's smart management," said Sky Sports' Roy Keane before kick-off in Madrid. "This is the perfect time for Trafford to come in, against top players, and show what he's capable of doing."
Trafford had little to do up until Elliot Anderson's sending-off in the 63rd minute. Spain had not even registered a shot on target at that point. The 24-year-old's only duties were occasional goal kicks and passes as the hosts struggled to get close to his goal.
But it all changed when Anderson departed. Suddenly, Trafford had to contend with swarming red shirts and a flurry of shots.
His focus didn't waver. His biggest contribution was his double save in stoppage time, when he dived to his right to deny Fermin Lopez then instantly pushed Mikel Oyarzabal's follow-up around the post.
"Every time you watch goalkeepers doing drills, it's that, making the save and then the reaction," said Keane, marvelling at the speed of his reflexes. Trafford was mobbed by team-mates afterwards.
But he had already kept Spain at bay on several occasions before that. In the 74th minute, he denied Lopez following a corner. He could do little about Spain's second goal, scored at close-range by Nico Williams from Lamine Yamal's perfect centre.
But Trafford was alert to save from Lamine Yamal shortly after that. He then got to his feet, in similar style to his double save in stoppage time, to prevent Marc Cucurella's angled shot from creeping in.
"Very good," added Tuchel in his press conference. "That's his job, to close the gap. We want competition in all positions."
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
"The obvious save, where he deserves full credit, is the double save at the very end. Absolutely brilliant."
But the England boss also highlighted the importance of his composure in possession. "There was a lot to do in the deep build-up as well, which he did very, very well, with everyone around him.
"Never lose the concentration, never lose the focus, never lose the vision where to find the free men to overcome the press and put the game to the opponent's half.
"With everyone else, he was part of a fantastic team performance."
Trafford's ball-playing ability was moulded in Manchester City's academy and with England's youth sides. His saves, meanwhile, were a continuation of his club performances this season.
According to underlying data from Opta, Trafford ranks top among all Premier League goalkeepers for goals prevented this season, having only conceded eight times for Leeds from shots worth 12.40 expected goals, giving him a score of 4.40.
It should be noted that Pickford also has a positive differential, having conceded 10 goals from shots worth 11.05 expected goals. He is eight years older than Trafford, at 32, but clearly has plenty left to offer. "There's not much between them," said Keane.
In addition to have 94 senior caps to Trafford's five, he has 372 Premier League appearances behind him. But a comparison of their numbers shows similar figures for percentage of shots saved.
Their styles differ in terms of their distribution, with Trafford sending a lower percentage of passes long, although that is partly explained by the differences in the way their respective clubs play.
For Tuchel, Trafford's impact can only be positive. He insisted there is no first-choice. But that in itself shows the dynamic has changed. Trafford looks ready for more opportunities - and having thwarted the world champions, they might come sooner rather than later.

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli says he draws on the influence of legendary manager Louis van Gaal in his own coaching career.
The Belgian played under the Dutchman during their time at AZ Alkmaar, a special period for Pocognoli during which he won the Eredivisie title in 2009.
Van Gaal also previously took charge of the Netherlands, and now that he has moved into international football himself, the Scotland boss reflected on the 75-year-old's influence.
"I take a lot from all of my gaffers, but probably he was the one with the most experience," Pocognoli told BBC Scotland.
"I was very young and you know in that moment he had all the Barcelona young players between his hands, also Ajax players.
"The way that he treats the young players in a direct way, honest way and hard way was for me really inspiring in my daily job now.
"I was lucky to have a lot of good coaches but he was probably the most that impressed me day by day, and I felt progress under him.
Progress is exactly what every Scotland fan is yearning for. Under Steve Clarke, the amount of that very commodity plateaued.
Years in the international wilderness were expelled with two European Championships and a World Cup appearance, but they were punctuated by disappointing results and dour tactics.
Pocognoli's arrival signified not only a new era, but a new approach, formation, selection and outlook.
It has been far from straightforward for the Belgian as he approaches 100 days in charge next week. Five games, two wins over North Macedonia, a draw in Slovenia and two humbling defeats mark his tenure so far.
Within it, a fresh system and injection of different faces to offer a break from the norm, but also plenty signs that a transformation will not be an immediate reality.
Scotland's failings in front of goal has remained, while it is clear the Scots are still getting to grips with a back three, albeit with enforced changes in personnel.
"Everything in life takes time to build if you want to achieve something," said Pocognoli.
"So we know that in the performance world everything goes faster and quicker, but we have an objective and we know that we have to go through the up and down and the good moments. At the end I hope that all this experience can make us stronger.
"I don't ask the players to be patient, it's just to believe in what we are doing."
Pocognoli acknowledges he's not had much opportunity to immerse himself in Scottish culture after taking his first foray into international management.
A wander around Glasgow is about all he's managed. And any further exploring will have to wait until after Monday's Nations League test in St Gallen.
Finishing in the top two of their group seems a tall order for Scotland, who are requiring a win and snookers in Slovenia. It seems progression to the next Euros will instead roll on to the qualifying campaign next year.
"We don't have the control of what will happen because Slovenia will decide," Pocognoli said. "But if we want to have a chance to go through to the group stage and to go to the play-offs we have to go with the bravery and try to play with courage and try to force something.
"I don't believe that we are waiting for something then it will happen, so let's go through our quality and try to be aggressive and wait what happens in Slovenia."

Mario Frick has been announced as the new head coach of Aberdeen, taking over from the sacked Stephen Robinson to become the club's fourth manager in 2026.
Capped 125 times as a striker for Liechtenstein, the 52-year-old was last in charge at Luzern, leaving the Swiss club in the summer after five years.
He follows Robinson, Peter Leven and Jimmy Thelin in leading the side in this calendar year and will take charge for the first time against Scottish Premiership bottom side Kilmarnock on Saturday.
"Throughout our discussions, he demonstrated a clear vision, strong leadership qualities and a deep understanding of what is required to build a successful team," said Pittodrie chief executive Adrian Bevington.
"He was also exceptionally well regarded by the many people across the game we consulted during the process, and the board was unanimous in its belief that he is the right person to lead Aberdeen forward."
Former Motherwell and St Mirren boss Robinson was dismissed on 9 November, with Aberdeen second bottom of the table and having lost four games in a row in all competitions.
'Aberdeen hunt yet another manager after ill-fated Robinson reign'
Watch new Aberdeen boss Frick score against Scotland in September 2010
Frick, who also managed Vaduz in the Swiss Super League, will be assisted by Roman Matter and is the seventh permanent manager since Dave Cormack took control of the club in November 2019.
As a player, his former clubs include FC Basel, FC Zurich, St. Gallen and Grasshopper, while his 16 international goals make him Liechtenstein's all-time top scorer.
"Mario is a strong personality with clear ideas about how he wants his teams to play," added sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel. "He brings energy, ambition and a winning mentality, and knows how to build a strong team environment.
"We were looking for the right person to lead the next chapter of Aberdeen FC, and I'm convinced Mario has the qualities, character and vision to make a real impact."
Frick got Vaduz promoted in 2020 before helping Luzern avoid relegation following his move there in 2021.
The next again year he guided them to a fourth-placed finish and European qualification, although they were knocked out of Conference League qualifying by Lee Johnson's Hibernian.
Aberdeen say Frick "has built a strong reputation for transforming teams, handing top-flight debuts to more than 30 academy players during his coaching career".
Hibs striker Thibault Klidje and current Aberdeen goalkeeper Marius Muller both played under him.
Aberdeen did not disclose contract details for Frick as he takes over a side with just three wins from 12 Premiership outings this season.
One of his international goals came at Hampden Park in 2010 when a late Stephen McManus header rescued a 2-1 win for Scotland.

Yeşilçam filmlerinin tanınan oyuncularında Şehnaz Dilan, uzun bir aranın ardından İstanbul Nişantaşı'nda görüntülendi.
Kendisini görüntüleyen basın mensuplarıyla sohbet eden 66 yaşındaki oyuncu, son görüntüsü ve açıklamalarıyla gündeme geldi.
Dilan'a, oyuncu Ediz Hun'un Yeşilçam'ın artık bittiği yönündeki sözleri soruldu. Açıklamaya alındığını belirten oyuncu, Yeşilçam'ın son kuşağının temsilcilerinin hala hayatta olduğunu söyledi.
"Biz daha ölmedik" ifadelerini kullanan Dilan şunları söyledi:
"Biraz alındım. Ediz Hun'un zamanındaki Yeşilçam bitti. En son kuşak benim ama... 200'e yakın dizi ve film çektik. Daha biz ölmedik, abilerim var yaşayan. Yeşilçam ölmedi, ben onu yaşatmaya çalışıyorum. Talihsiz açıklama olarak görüyorum. Onların kuşak tamam ama biz onlardan sonra geldik. Yeşilçam ölmedi!"
1960'ta İzmir'de dünyaya gelen Şehnaz Dilan'ın gerçek adı Şehnaz Vreskala. Oyunculuk kariyerinden önce sporla ilgilenen Dilan, gençlik yıllarında İzmir Filizspor'da futbol oynadı. Kadın futbolunun öncü takımlarından biri olan kulüpte kaptanlık görevini de üstlendi.
Takımın fahri başkanlığını ise Yeşilçam oyuncularından Filiz Akın yapıyordu. Futbol oynadığı dönemde fotomodellik de yapan Dilan, 1982 yılında İstanbul'a taşındı ve sinema kariyerine adım attı.
Yeşilçam'da farklı yapımlarda kamera karşısına geçen Şehnaz Dilan, Kemal Sunal'ın başrolünde yer aldığı Yoksul filminde Leyla karakterini canlandırdı. Filmde, Sunal'ın hayat verdiği karakterin nişanlısı olarak izleyici karşısına çıktı.
Dilan, Şener Şen ile birlikte rol aldığı Aşık Oldum filmindeki Kırmızı Kadın karakteriyle de tanındı. Oyuncunun yer aldığı diğer yapımlar arasında Kızlar Sınıfı ve Umut Sokağı da bulunuyor.

Harry Kane scored for a record-equalling seventh England away game
Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday.
In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions.
Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular."
To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of under-statement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular.
It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations Cup final.
If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment.
The question being asked when England held a one-goal advantage through Harry Kane's penalty at half-time was 'what would theirs and Tuchel's reaction be?' Stick or twist?
Would Tuchel tell England to press their foot on the pedal for acceleration? Or would he take the approach of going into reverse gear, as he did to ill-fated effect against Argentina?
How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?
Who swaggered around like he owned the place? Spain v England ratings
The answer was delivered when they added goals from Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White in the first 12 minutes of the second half.
This being England, they then created a mess for themselves when Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the area after 65 minutes, although the main culprit was Jarell Quansah for initially conceding possession.
Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and, when Yamal set up Nico Williams for Spain's second with 15 minutes left, it looked like more than an hour of faultless England football might be wasted.
But not a bit of it, as goalkeeper James Trafford produced heroics and England defended with every fibre to close out this landmark win.
Was this the statement victory that was almost demanded of Tuchel as recompense for the World Cup disappointment, a performance to convince the doubters?
"We're fully aware what we put out there," said Tuchel afterwards. "What a performance we put out for 65 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up.
"Of course, the red card and the penalty changed the momentum and the characteristics of the game... but we know, and the players know very, very well, what they put out there. That is the statement - and that is the significance of this victory."
Simple details of the game barely touch the sides of a night filled with quality and glorious chaos, vindication for Tuchel and England's positive approach.
Spain opened with an ostentatious parade of the World Cup in front of England's players as the teams lined up, perhaps a psychological reminder of the superiority that has seen them dominate international football.
What followed, at times literally, reduced Spain's supporters to stunned silence and their players to a shell-shocked shambles chasing the shadows that were overpowering them.
England's white shirts were everywhere but Spain could not get near them. The tormentors had become the tormented.
It was alien territory for a Spain side that has carried all before them, while England's fans tucked away high in a corner of this vast arena were equally unbelieving as a dream unfolded in front of them.
England, for 65 minutes, were in a different class to Spain. And, yes, you have read that right.
From the first whistle, employing a suffocatingly high press, England ran all over Spain.
When White crowned a superb move with the third goal four minutes after Konsa's second, it looked, remarkably, to be a case of how big England's victory margin would be.
In the end, the margin was narrow but the stature and significance of England's victory was huge.
Tuchel labelled this meeting with Spain as "proof of concept at the highest level".
There was no doubt the German manager and England were under fierce scrutiny after the manner of the collapse, mentally and tactically, against Argentina at the World Cup.
Here they delivered the proof they can match the best then beat them.
If the vital signs were being forensically examined for evidence Tuchel has learned lessons from a chastening World Cup, that England have improved after that harrowing experience, this game delivered these conclusions.
Of course, England must do it again. Do it when the pressure and expectation in at its highest.
The Nations League is competitive but cannot be compared to a World Cup and European Championship, both titles currently in the possession of the team they beat here.
But England's world-class players delivered - Kane inevitably with his 93rd international goal, but Jude Bellingham was on a level of his own, the outstanding performer on both sides with an individual display simply confirming he is the player with everything.
And Tuchel got his big calls right, especially selecting Trafford, who responded superbly in a frantic closing phase. White, making a strong claim for the right-back berth, not only scored a goal but produced crucial challenges in the face of relentless, albeit belated, Spain pressure.
"This was the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness," said Tuchel. "It was on the highest level football wise in all aspects of the game. We did everything that needs to be done together.
"The deep build-up. The high press. The counter-attack. The tracking. The defensive phases. This was an excellent performance and of course a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.
"We overcame some difficult moments in the end. That's how it is. But we are very well aware which steps we took now through after the World Cup."
England's win means they top their Nations League group, but the importance spreads much wider than simply a league table.
The first 65 minutes were simply breathtaking. Spain wilting under attack after attack. Spain rattled until they shook as England refused to allow them meaningful possession.
After Anderson's dismissal, bad memories were revisited as England were forced into a rearguard action, but any other result than the one that was eventually delivered would have been a huge injustice.
England survived 29 nervous minutes, including added time, to make a powerful statement about their current status, which is much healthier than when recriminations about Tuchel's approach provided the post-World Cup narrative.
"I'm very impressed with the steps that we took after the World Cup", said Tuchel. "We wanted to get better, better in a deep build-up, get better in defending in a low block and, on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play against every opponent.
"I think this was clearly visible throughout the whole group phase. The results followed with an excellent group phase."
Was this the finest performance of Tuchel's time in charge? Most observers felt so, but the head coach was best placed to answer.
"Yes, given the circumstances," he said, "and the pressure, the quality, where we played in this building against the reigning world champions, unbeaten in 43 matches. Putting a performance out there in Madrid, and in this environment, was a very complete performance."
Tuchel will, of course, need repeat performances - but the outstanding ability and character England displayed here to beat the World Cup holders will deliver a huge injection of confidence and self-belief.

Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding
In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: s omehow, anyhow . What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too.
Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch.
As they went there was celebration for them, applause for all of them, Spain too. What a game it had been, what a night. “We knew we would beat them,” Declan Rice claimed afterwards. Would? Maybe in the 60th minute they had known, England 3-0 up and playing their way to a superb and, yes, comfortable victory over the world champions – the first team to beat them, penalties aside, in 44 games and almost a thousand nights. But with half an hour left Spain had been revived, England reduced to 10 men and, as Tuchel said: “Thirty minutes against Spain feels like three hours.”
It did to him, to his players too. To everyone else, it flew by. This is the best game you can see in football, Spain’s head coach, Luis de la Fuente, had said, and he wasn’t wrong. When England got that third, the fans had sung: “You’ve seen the England, now eff off home.” Nah, you’re all right, thanks. Far better to stay and watch this; it had been hugely impressive from England; now, here were Spain too. Now, it was going to be wild. Nervy, noisy and fun .
Jarell Quansah lost the ball, Fermín López released Lamine Yamal and Spain won a penalty that Mikel Oyarzabal scored. It was some game. Twice Spain scored; countless times they came, the Metropolitano chanting: “Yes, we can!” In the end, they could not, but they had got close. They had really believed they might; as the momentum built, perhaps they had really believed they would.
This was history: made by England, perhaps; broken by England, certainly. Spain had not been beaten in 90 or 120 minutes since Colombia defeated them two and a half years ago, their only loss in that period coming on penalties against Portugal in last year’s Nations League final . They had not lost a competitive game since Scotland in March 2023 . That, Fifa said, was the longest run ever and even if there was an asterisk, it was still mightily impressive, but it had to end some time. If not necessarily like this.
“With every passing game, defeat gets closer,” De la Fuente said. Now, it arrived. “They can seem invincible but we’re ready,” Tuchel had said. At the end Spain’s staff lined up to applaud their players off. England’s players stood before their fans, exhausted, arms raised.
Italy went into their clash in Brussels top of Group A1 after their 3-1 win against France on Thursday but came crashing back to Earth as they were comfortably beaten by Belgium .
Pio Esposito gave Italy ⁠an early lead but their joy was short-lived as Belgium scored ​three times before the ​interval through Maxim De Cuyper, ​Nathan Ngoy and Jérémy Doku (pictured). Diego Moreira made it 4-1 in the 80th minute.
France beat Turkey 2-1 in Bordeaux ​thanks to an own ‌goal by Emirhan ​Topcu and ​an effort by Bournemouth's Eli Junior Kroupi, meaning they won the group with 13 points, ahead of Belgium who ended on 12. Italy, on 10 points, missed out.
England and Spain had already confirmed qualification to the quarter-finals before Sunday's dramatic clash between the sides in Madrid, which England won 3-2 , but the remaining match in Group A3 saw Croatia beat Czechia 2-1, thanks to Lovro Majer's 87th-minute winner.
In Group C1, Albania sealed top spot and promotion to League B after a 2-0 win over Belarus in Budapest. Rey Manaj and Elseid Hysaj scored goals in each half. Finland ended their campaign in the group with a 7-2 thumping of San Marino in Helsinki, headlined by a hat-trick by forward Adrian Svanbäck. San Marino are relegated to League D after failing to register a single point from their six games, ending with a goal difference of -22.
In Group C2, Montenegro completed an unbeaten group campaign with a 4-1 victory in Cyprus . Genoa forward Milutin Osmajic got them off to a fast start in the fifth minute while Nikola Krstocic added a second-half double. Armenia and already-relegated Latvia played out a goalless draw in Riga. Reuters and Guardian sport
Ultimately, this came in two acts. The first act was superb from England, the second heroic. “We can’t play like them and they can’t play like us,” De la Fuente had said and yet what was so striking about the way that this began was that England took the game to Spain on their own terms. They were the ones dominating the ball, not allowing their opponents out; theirs was the midfield, the control.
Ten minutes is not a reliable sample size it is true – and it turned out even an hour might not have been enough – but as the clock rolled into double figures, the possession stat showed 70% for England. While that number fell, when it reached 20 the shot count was 4-0. The first came after 39 seconds and before Spain had a touch, Unai Simón flashing out a right hand to Jude Bellingham’s shot inside the six-yard box. Martín Zubimendi immediately had to stop Anthony Gordon’s shot and then Simón stopped Rice. All that inside three minutes; three more and Kane was flashing a shot just wide.
England’s fans were enjoying this. A chorus of “the best in the world, the best in the world, Harry Kane, the best in the world” came down. They watched England control Spain’s place, Elliot Anderson and Rice excelling. They watched England take the lead, Kane scoring his 93rd goal with penalty No 28. They watched Bellingham burst through, responding by launching into a rendition of the Beatles which was still going when they watched Ezri Konsa head in the second. Then they watched Bellingham burst through again to set up Ben White. They watched England be brilliant for an hour but there was still plenty of Spain to watch as well. Nervously now and they will remember Trafford’s superhero rescue for some time, but it was still their night, and what a night.

After a week dominated by a headline-grabbing stadium imbroglio , Gotham FC and the Kansas City Current finally got down to the vital business of their NWSL semi-final on Sunday afternoon, a frigid encounter at an unlikely venue on New York City’s Randall’s Island with a place in next Saturday’s championship match at stake.
Haley Hopkins delivered the knockout blow at the death, hitting an 89th-minute volley off the crossbar and in to seal a 2-1 upset that shattered Gotham FC’s bid for the league’s first-ever treble. Paired with Croix Bethune’s first-half free-kick stunner, the late winner sent fourth-seeded Kansas City past the NWSL Shield and in-season Challenge Cup winners into a championship showdown in six days against the Washington Spirit.
On a windswept afternoon where unyielding gusts undercut the warmth of a near-cloudless 50F sky, a physical opening stretch produced six fouls in the first eight minutes before either side threatened. Gotham recorded the first shot after 12 minutes when Jaedyn Shaw ran onto a Guro Reiten pass and missed wide right. Kansas City answered three minutes later, with Malawian star Temwa Chawinga firing wide left from the center of the area.
Twenty minutes in, Bethune won a free kick 25 yards out after a foul by Denise O’Sullivan. Stepping up with her left foot, she coolly curled her strike around the Gotham wall and inches inside the post . The goal from Bethune, the NWSL’s midfielder of the year two seasons ago with Washington, left the crowd in stunned silence before a smattering of boos echoed around the ground.
The popular Rose Lavelle came on after half-time for O’Sullivan to deafening swells and made an immediate impact, winning a couple of free kicks and nearly finding the equalizer with a left-footed shot from the center of the area that missed wide left. But opportunities came fewer and further between over the next quarter-hour as the current tightened their defensive shell.
Kansas City coach Chris Armas said his team had deliberately traded their customary high press for a more conservative mid-block designed to deny Gotham space. “We knew this game would be much more suited for the mid-block,” he said. The approach paid off: Gotham would finish the match without a shot on target.
With their repeat bid hanging in the balance, Gotham found an equalizer against the run of play in the 69th minute when Midge Purce whipped in a cross that ricocheted between goalkeeper Lorena and defender Gabrielle Robinson before caroming off Laney Rouse into her own net – leveling the match at one apiece despite the hosts still not having registered a single shot on target. It was hardly a match for the artistry of Bethune’s silky opener, but the delirious home crowd was in no mood to quibble.
The contest appeared bound for extra time past sundown with temperatures plunging. But Gotham, having scraped through last week’s quarter-final on another own goal, were suddenly within reach of a second straight NWSL final without having scored a goal of their own in either playoff match. Hopkins had other ideas, delivering the dramatic decider in the 89th minute before adding insult to injury by blowing kisses to the crowd from the touchline, provoking a cacophony of boos.
Armas later revealed that the winner came from a set-piece routine months in the making, with assistant coach Lucas Rodriguez spotting space at the back post and captain Lo’eau LaBonta calling the play. “Haley Hopkins gets the finish, and not an easy one on the left foot, but well executed,” he said.
With its solitary grandstand, roofline lettering and towering floodlights, 5,000-seat Icahn Stadium gave the appearance of an 1890s English football ground dropped beneath the Triborough Bridge – an improbable stage for one of the biggest matches of the NWSL season.
Gotham had been forced to abandon their usual home at Sports Illustrated Stadium in Harrison, New Jersey, amid concerns over the deteriorating playing surface. The relocation capped a chaotic week for the league, which found itself juggling stadium availability, network television commitments and player safety at the most consequential stage of its season. Gotham’s regular ground, owned by MLS’s New York Red Bulls, had been booked for a friendly against Mexico’s Club América on Saturday, further complicating an already untenable situation.
Ultimately, the club prioritized a playable pitch over capacity. At one-fifth the size of their usual home, the municipal track venue where Usain Bolt made a creaky run-up to the Rio Olympics created an awkward compromise: world-class stars competing on a stage resembling a relic of football’s distant past. Sunday’s meeting also carried the unmistakable flavor of revenge. A year ago, Gotham entered the playoffs as the eighth seed and stunned the top-seeded Current in the quarter-finals, ending Kansas City’s 18-match home win streak on a dramatic extra-time goal from Katie Lampson before going on to claim their second NWSL crown in three seasons .
This time the roles were reversed, with Gotham the top seeds and Kansas City arriving as dangerous floaters. The fourth-seeded Current had run off six consecutive wins entering Sunday, including a 1-0 extra-time victory over Angel City in the quarter-finals, settled by Michelle Cooper’s 96th-minute penalty. “There was an element of vengeance,” Hopkins said afterward. “We knew it was going to be our hardest game of the year.”
But 12 months after watching Gotham end their season in heartbreaking fashion, Kansas City returned the favor, halting the hosts’ bid for a fourth title in the club’s two-decade history. Next stop: Washington, where a chance to capture their first-ever NWSL crown awaits.

Kitap dünyasına açılan kapınızı aralayın! En sevdiğiniz kitapları indirimli fiyatlarla keşfedin ve hayal gücünüzü genişletin.
Gaziantep FK 'de başkan Memik Yılmaz , teknik direktör Volkan Demirel ile prensipte anlaştıklarını söyledi.
Yılmaz, bir otelde düzenlediği basın buluşmasında, takım olarak en çok kenetlenmeye ihtiyaç duydukları zaman diliminden geçtiklerini dile getirdi.
Takım için en iyi teknik direktörü bulmaya çalıştıklarını belirten Yılmaz, " Volkan Demirel ile prensipte anlaştık. Yarın takımın başında antrenmana çıkacak " ifadelerini kullandı.
Futbolculuk kariyerinin ardından Fenerbahçe'de antrenör olarak görev yapan Volkan Demirel, ilk teknik direktörlük deneyimini Aralık 2021'de Fatih Karagümrük'te yaşadı. Demirel, daha sonra Eylül 2022'de Hatayspor'un başına geçti ve Mayıs 2024'e kadar bu görevini sürdürdü.
2024-2025 sezonunda Bodrum FK'yi çalıştıran Demirel'in son durağı ise Gençlerbirliği oldu. Başkent ekibinde 2025-2026 sezonunda iki ayrı dönemde görev alan teknik direktörün son sözleşmesi Mayıs 2026'da sona erdi.

texts.https://www.haberler.com/haberler/phil-c:
İngiliz müzisyen Phil Collins, cumartesi akşamı Los Angeles'taki Peacock Theater'da düzenlenen törenle Rock and Roll Hall of Fame'e solo sanatçı olarak kabul edildi. Collins, daha önce Genesis grubunun üyesi olarak da bu onura layık görülmüştü.
Collins'i sahneye Blink-182 grubunun davulcusu Travis Barker davet etti. Sağlık sorunları nedeniyle 2022'deki Genesis veda turnesinden bu yana sahneye çıkmayan 75 yaşındaki sanatçı, iki bastonla kürsüye yürüdü ve salondakiler tarafından ayakta alkışlandı.
Euronews'ün aktardığına göre Collins, mikrofonu aldığında "Göründüğüm kadar kötü değilim" dedi. Ünlü müzisyen, "Benden son duyduğunuz bu olmayacak, size söz verebilirim" diye ekledi.
Konuşması sırasında duygulanan Collins'i törende, oyuncu Lily Collins'in de aralarında bulunduğu çocukları izledi. Gecede Cynthia Erivo, sanatçının "In The Air Tonight" şarkısını seslendirirken Travis Barker da parçanın davul bölümünü çaldı.
Collins, tören sonrasında gazetecilere yaptığı açıklamada "Hayatım birbiri ardına gelen olaylardan, birbiri ardına gerçekleşen hayallerden ibaret oldu" dedi.
Aynı gece Wu-Tang Clan, Billy Idol, Queen Latifah, MC Lyte, Joy Division/New Order ve hayatını kaybeden Luther Vandross da Rock and Roll Hall of Fame'e kabul edildi. Bu yılın listesinde yer alan Oasis, Sade ve Iron Maiden ise törene katılmadı.
Haberler.com'da yer alan yorumlar, kullanıcıların kişisel görüşlerini yansıtır ve haberler.com'un editöryal politikası ile örtüşmeyebilir. Yorumların hukuki sorumluluğu tamamen yazarlarına aittir.
